storm.summary_layperson: A severe thunderstorm watch covers the wider NYC/lower Hudson Valley area tonight, and radar shows several strong cells 25-38 miles off to the west and southwest, but the Sound isn't offering the cove any of its usual protection this evening.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound (75°F) is actually warmer than the air (73°F) tonight, not cooler — the marine-layer gap is already negative and stays negative through the whole overnight series, so there's no protective buffer to lean on.
storm.detail_html:
OKX has a severe thunderstorm watch in effect for the NYC metro area, northeast New Jersey, and the Lower Hudson Valley until midnight. Radar out of KOKX shows a cluster of cells at 42–61 dBZ arrayed 25–38 miles to the west, southwest, and north of the cove — strong storms by reflectivity, though most of the closest ones (25–30 mi SW/WSW/W) are currently moving away or holding roughly steady relative to the cove rather than closing.

The local modifier that usually helps here — a cool marine layer sitting under warm air — isn't available tonight. Sound water is running about 75°F, roughly 2°F warmer than the 73°F air, which is backwards from what a stabilizing marine layer needs. The air-water gap trend confirms this holds (or gets worse) through the entire evening and overnight series, never crossing back above the threshold that would create a buffer. The sea breeze isn't a factor either — only about 5% of coastal stations are showing any onshore/southerly component, well short of what a thermal circulation needs.

The one cell actually closing on the cove is 37 miles NNE at 42 dBZ, closing at 23 kt, projected to arrive around 7:43 PM with a window of 7:22–8:04 PM. Because neither the marine layer nor the sea breeze has anything left to give by that time, the arrival model applied zero late-stretch to this cell — it should arrive close to on-schedule and at close to full strength, not weakened or delayed the way the cove's evening storms sometimes are.

Net for the cove vs. surrounding towns: expect roughly the same risk as the rest of the watch area tonight, not the usual coastal discount. The most likely flashpoint is that ~7:40–8:00 PM window if the northern cell holds its track; the SW/WSW cluster near 25–30 miles is a lower near-term concern while it's moving away, but bears watching in case it redevelops or turns back toward the cove before the watch expires at midnight.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 37 mi NNE closing at 23 kt, arriving after both the marine layer and the sea breeze have already faded for the night — expect it near full strength with no local buffer.

wind.tactics_blurb: This is a gradient-wind evening, not a sea-breeze day — expect a slow backing ENE-to-NE flow in the 9–14 kt range with no thermal shift to play. Favor the right/east side of the course, where open-Sound stations are showing noticeably more pressure than the sheltered cove mouth.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today doesn't qualify as a sea-breeze day: only about 5% of coastal stations show any onshore component, well under what the thermal circulation needs, and the air-water temperature contrast doesn't come close to its gate either. So everything in this window is background gradient flow, not a thermal sea breeze, and the sea-breeze direction-maturation correction does not apply.

HRRR has that gradient wind holding ENE around 10–11 kt through sunset (7:26 PM), then gradually backing to NE by 8–9 PM and continuing to back toward NNE while easing to around 9 kt by 10 PM. This slow counterclockwise backing lines up with the broader storm system parked to the west tonight — expect a gentle veer-back-and-fade rather than a sharp shift.

There's a real model/observation gap worth flagging: nearby open-Sound stations are running noticeably stronger than either HRRR or the cove's own instrument right now. A station 3 miles east on open water is reading a sustained 18 kt ENE gusting to 24 kt, while Riverside YC at the cove mouth shows only 6.7 kt sustained (9.7 kt 10-minute average) gusting 18 kt, and HRRR's own forecast for this hour is just under 11 kt. That's a real exposure effect — the cove itself is sheltered relative to the open Sound just outside it — not sensor noise.

Given that, favor the right/east side of the course, where the fuller open-water pressure is showing up first, and plan for the wind to keep backing left (ENE → NE → NNE) through the window rather than swing back right.

Fleet impact: 9–14 kt with gusts into the high teens is solid moderate breeze for the fleet — no big shifts to play beyond the slow backing trend, so steady starts and working the pressure on the right will matter more than chasing shifts.
